comment_text.value:
1) Opportunity cost mostly. I suffer from a _debilitating_ case of zero-sum thinking. "If I'm doing X, I'm not doing Y." Weightlifting isn't (overly) boring/painful; I'd just much rather be programming, by far my favorite activity. It's uncomfortable, but my physical pain tolerance is fairly high. Boring is solved by having a podcast/audiobook going, but for the "big lifts" I prefer silence to focus.

2) I don't use motivation or discipline. I use habit. I'm fairly busy, so my mantra is "bias towards action". I could sit there and stew about how much I hate the upcoming workout... or I can wake up, do my morning routine to an audiobook/podcast, eat breakfast while happily programming, NOT thinking about the day's workout, then transition sharply into it. When it's time, I just fucking do it. It's like flossing. I don't even have it on a schedule, because I don't want to think about "gotta start at X time". It starts when I reach a natural stopping point shortly after breakfast, whenever that is. I have literally never missed a workout in years so _something's_ working. (To be clear, there are obvious exceptions for travel/holidays/etc, I'm talking missing a workout due to a lack of "character".)

It helps that my gym is literally in the same room as my devbox. I launch a Claude prompt/whatever, do a set, repeat. Instead of doomscrolling between sessions, I bias towards action. I keep myself too busy to think about how much I don't want to exercise. The only time I let myself think about "god I hate this" is when I'm seconds from psyching myself up for a big lift. I know that if I let myself, I'll just stew and stew and grumble and bitch and make excuses. So I don't give myself that mental space. There's virtually 0 time between my favorite activity, then context switching to "alright let's get this". No space for the "ulgh" emotion to creep in.

To use an MCU Avenger's analogy, I'm _always_ angry. I'm always hate exercise. But I box it with what I love (programming), so I switch back and forth with zero time for the emotion to permeate. For a moment I'm a normal happy programmer, then seconds later I stand up, take a breath, and go Hulk mode.

Is that discipline? IDK. It doesn't feel like I'm bare-knuckle-holding-on-perserevering-despite-all-odds. I just don't mentallay dwell on it, and when my non-vibed custom exercise tracker beeps (it predates LLMs), saying it's been 3-4 minutes and I need to do the next set, I happily ignore it, finish my thought/prompt, then do the damned lift.

---

Negativity over, my favorite exercise is Zone 2 because the inclined treadmill is at my standing desk and I can happily work while being in The Zone (in both senses). Zone 2 is the best. A cheap $50 Craigslist treadmill + standing desk will burn an absolute fuckton of calories once you figure out how to walk (really its more a march) and type at the same time. Honestly I could (and have) Zone 2ed for up to 3hrs/day for weeks at a time. I reduced that because I got tired of eating so much food lol. Zone 2 is the best.

Then there's the weekly Nordic 4 by 4 which I apply the weightliftng mentality to.

comment_text.value:
50+, terrible at brushing and oral hygene in general. Actually lived in the jungle for years, almost like a caveman. 25+ years without a single dentist visit. Was in Thailand last spring, went to a dentistry shop in the mall as a walk-in, paid about 45 dollars for a deep cleaning and panoramic x-ray. Other than some startlingly crunky plaque in the rinse and spit cycles, zero cavities, zero need for intervention. It all comes down to the microbiome. I blame the complete lack of 'antiseptic' mouthwash and other interventions that skew the microbial populations, combined with just plain good luck.

I refuse to use antibiotic soaps either. I reserve the tools of sterility for the space in front of my laminar flow hood and the like when preparing live cultures for cheeses and brews. I lived where fluoridated water was a practice during my early years when my teeth had formed - as that's actually when the flouride has the most impact...once the teeth are built, there's little effect from consuming flouride on the enamel.

Later in late grade-school I lived in a place where fluoridated water had not happened, and so the school was doing a routine annual flouride mouth rinse-and-spit routine in the class. Was a 'conscientious objector' causing some chagrin for the teachers, they would pass out the little cup of chemical brew and start the timer, while i just stared at the paper cup and got threatened with having to write "I will ...." sentences as punishment. Even that didn't really have any impact on my actions. Adding another hashmark by my name on the blackboard as a tally of pages of meaningless repetitive sentences which I would never actually do or turn in. That had zero leverage against my test scores or passing any subject. So what if I couldn't go out to recess to sweat on a bare dirt playground with zero swings or other appeal. Fine by me.

But, by 3rd grade I already had my own two-stage steromicroscope and was acutely aware of the need for balanced microbiomes in all of life, learning about soil and aquatic microbiomes from my grandfather. So, very much not the normal kid.

All that aside, my gums could use more care, so I'm trying to be more diligent and brush daily with salt, baking soda and the tiniest bit of fennel and mint oil. Its showing some improvement.

The most damning comment I've ever gotten out of a dentist when dealing with the obvious malpractice of another was, "Well, that's not how I would have done it, but philosophies vary.". This wasn't merely fear of being sued by the subject of criticism. Dental associations routinely prohibit criticism of peers. If a dentist honestly assesses the bad practices of their peers to a client, they could lose their job before any of those they criticize.

People need to realize this. Good dentists often can't call out bad ones without shouldering significant risk to themselves. You have to pay attention to what your dentist is doing and get a second opinion when it seems appropriate. That second opinion should be as independent as possible. Preferably from a different clinic, and the dentist should not be informed of the previous opinion. If they know they're contradicting another dentist, they may play it safe.

I've had similar experiences. It's kind of terrifying, actually, you have to walk the line of being annoying enough to get what you want but not so annoying they completely ignore you.

One of the things I've learned is to apply the Socratic method, preferably in front of their colleagues if they try to brush you off. Also, if you've got scary symptoms, demand they write down what your symptoms are on your record and why they aren't concerned, then demand a copy of all relevant records (it's your property) -- this often gets them to reevaluate your risk in terms of their career.

Worst case scenario, you can make up medical history. I had a family member pass recently from colorectal cancer. They had symptoms but their PCP kept insisting they were too young. My family member suddenly "remembered" her aunt died of CRC when she was a kid. This got her referred to a gastroenterologist, and they found out she was stage 4...after her PCP delayed her diagnosis for like a year. She actually had grounds for a malpractice suit but who's got the energy or money for that when they're fighting stage 4 cancer?

Also, know your state's agency responsible for policing health insurance. This family member's insurance company routinely tried to deny life saving procedures, but a call to the right govt agency set them in line each time.

Oh that's neat. Yeah I got started on heroku too. Fly.io also comes to mind.

We run our own gitlab instance in a central AWS account that has some infra buckets containing modularized Terraform packaged into tarballs that are then fanned out to a couple hundred aws accounts across the teams and environments (prod, qual, dev).

Its all deployed via gitlab ci cd pipelines (which are just ec2 instances spawned at pipeline invocation) in multiple layers. The first layer is a foundation laying the networking rules and the IAM roles, permissions, policies and boundaries, some logging and monitoring. The second layer then assigns team specifics such as budget and maps people's accounts to roles depending on their access level (maintainer, developer, reporter). This layer can also be used to customize firewall rules like opening ports to the company internal IP ranges. The third and final layer is then all of the application infrastructure of the teams, so all their persistence, compute, load balancing, dns routing and serverless stuff. My prior teammates did a lot by hand in the aws console but I told them to stop and retain everything as IaC code. Besides Terraform, in my team we use Packer to build reusable "golden" machine images but also Ansible to configure live machines.

I'm still surprised nobody bothered us to change to Opentofu, it's not even been mentioned yet lol.

story_title.value: Neckbeard – A DevOps/platform/SRE plugin for your agent

I don't recall why I picked the FireGL versus the Quadro, I think the drivers looked better in 2001. I do recall we paid $2K for it which seemed like a lot at the time, but my personal annual budget for gfx cards is still $2K.

Even before that, I had this insane software OpenGL called MetroX which was a full replacement for XFree86 that had native OpenGL support, allowing me to port a molecular graphics package (MidasPlus) to Linux (at the time, the authors used expensive SGIs and Alpha workstations). Later, Mesa replaced MetroX and was fast enough to do routine modelling for smaller systems, and eventually, with nvida T&L we could finally do decent large scale modelling (although the program used lines, which typically were not well-accelerated on the lower end cards that I could afford). At that point, the group I worked with looked at my machine (a linux box with a consumer grade GPU) and looked at their SGIs (including the abysmal SGI Visual Workstation running NT) and Alphas and saw the writing on the wall and eventually switched to Linux as their primary platform.

It really was a perfect example of "first they laugh at you, then they fight you, then you win" for me.

story_title.value: Nvidia's first GPU: GeForce 256

With modern X ray imaging devices I feel like the dangers of irradiation from dental imaging are probably quite low. If nuclear hormesis holds up, you may actually be better off getting the imaging done.

The problem is the same as the CT scan: as much as my health anxiety would love another set of CT scans to feel relieved about, even if they do find something potentially interesting it may be worse to act on it than to do nothing, while leaving other things that can't show up on imaging unnoticed, potentially diverting attention and giving you a false sense of security.

YouTuber and doctor Dr. Bernard "Chubbyemu" Hsu recently covered an upsetting example to demonstrate how doing additional routine scans wouldn't have helped and may have harmed in a specific sort of scenario that I'm sure many of us fear from time to time. It doesn't prove or even assert that such scans would be useless, only that they are far from a panacea and that it isn't settled science that we'd be better off with it.

https://youtu.be/YDYMMgyN4k0

And to me, I think that ties into how we're doing dentistry wrong: I think taking routine X rays for patients with healthy mouths, no history of issues and no symptoms is reckless. Maybe it is sometimes beneficial, but every single year as a requirement seems insane. Why not every 3? Are we really catching things early or are we drilling into teeth that are fine? I question it.

Of course, I'm just some chuckle fuck on the Internet with zero dentistry experience, but my knee-jerk is that something seems off here.

story_title.value: Do dentists know what they're doing?

comment_text.value:
Just a few years ago, before the LLM-assisted-coding-era, I already did not like frameworks as much as I used to.

I liked Rails. But that was more because through Rails I learned the MVC pattern, learned the layer-middelware pattern from Rack (and the ActiveRecord ORM -- but I now no longer like ORMs but that's a different story). Those 2 pattern I still use today in some way or form, and I find them in many modern (Rust) web development frameworks/libs.

So I now no longer use Rails for new projects. These projects were all SSR web apps (traditional server-side rendered web apps that use JavaScript sparingly), built with Kotlin+http4k. Http4k is a web library, so no framework there and it feels very good.

The article is very frontend/JS-focussed. I prefer to keep things simpler and just use SSR for the UI. This is because above all (1) I dont like JavaScript (not even when my LLM writes it for me) and (2) for the type of application it is not needed to do state management again in the browser (IMHO it's just more code for the same features).

Sure, a little JS is needed in my apps too. But I (assisted by LLM) use it sparingly and when I use it it's with Alpine.js.

CSS with Tailwind and JS with Alpine makes for pages that are mostly "self contained" (the CSS and JS defined in the same place as the HTML that relates to it), which makes reasoning about them so much easier. For HTML building i use kotlinx.html (an HTML eDSL in Kotlin; HTML as Kotlin code).

I'd say http4k, Tailwind and Alpine are not frameworks. Maybe Alpine is most framework-like of all of these. At least they are not frameworks in the sense that they do not dictate my project folder structure and "how everything ties together".

With http4k the "how everything ties together" answer is in your own project's code, NOT in "the framework" or in 3rd party library code.

In my latest projects (all LLM assisted) I make heavy use of architecture tests: tests on the shape (e.g.: folder structure) of my codebase. These tests check that my architecture rules are adhered to. comment_text.value:
> "Let's consume more" for the poor. It is a grotesque argument.

OP was making a fair point that not everybody has the same amount of time and energy (or money) to tolerate shifts in their routine, which in the context of a "personal vs collective responsibility" style argument is entirely reasonable.

By the same token, if only the _rich_ have the freedom to make such behavior changes for the sake of conservation it will only ever have a token impact, and in many cases the "correct" level to make an efficiency pitch at is the community: a decent light rail system will always outperform everyone driving their own vehicle to work/the store/downtown in terms of space and energy efficiency.

...but, to get people to buy into such "collectivist" systems, you often have to get them to contend with some perceived reduction in personal convenience: yes, a train doesn't need a parking lot and uses less gas per passenger-mile, but then you're beholden to the train schedule. It's exactly _that_ sentiment that I find frustrating in advocating for sustainable civic design.

To OP's point: whatever that "collectivist" option is necessarily has to contend that standards of accessibility and convenience are not constant across the population. That doesn't inherently mean "the poor should consume more," but that "hang dry your laundry" isn't an option for everyone in the current dominant socioeconomic structure.

comment_text.value:
Rayhunter is a great tool, but unfortunately, it is only a passive monitor for cellular state changes and not an active defense.

Modern Stingrays / IMSI catchers support all standards up to 5G. They easily exploit 4G networks and 5G Non-Standalone (NSA) deployments. The only effective active defenses include (a) using a device locked strictly to 5G Standalone (SA) mode with SUCI (Subscription Concealed Identifier) enabled, preventing fallback to 4G/3G/2G where identity spoofing is trivial, (b) keeping the device in airplane mode most of the time, only going online briefly from unpredictable, shifting locations, and (c) using custom cellular baseband firmware that can reject anomalies (like a tower suddenly appearing too close or lacking neighbor cell lists), though this requires custom building your own solution as ready-made consumer solutions are hard to find. The last one can be achieved with Rayhunter, of course, but it would require some patching to Rayhunter and always carrying a mobile phone connected to the Rayhunter-supported Wi-Fi hotspot device.

Finally, intelligence mercenaries (and therefore LE agencies that contract them) use warrantless network-side exploits like SS7/Diameter attacks to remotely query the core telecom routing system and harvest the location of the tower target's phone is currently using¹ ². This doesn't even require sending legal DD requests to telcos to get target's cell tower.

[1] https://www.researchgate.net/publication/370809133_Attacks_t...

[2] https://www.lighthousereports.com/methodology/surveillance-s...

This is an interesting question! I'm not an expert in Orleans but I have looked at it alongside koka. The user defined key vs pid distinction is important and using a user defined key like in Orleans has advantages for keeping track of their virtual actors(grains). Their automatic lifecycle management is nice, but you really have to trust the runtime to know when something is really idle. I think their failure handling with auto state restoration is a mistake, recreating an actor with bad state is a recipe for crashes.

What I have that Orleans is missing is compile time protocol checking, typesd and hash checked remote calls, capability management, cluster authentication, and no stop the world GC. Orleans doesn't have choreography per se, they have sagas as a convention.

Yeah, GO routines are meant to solve different problems than share nothing actors.

This is exactly the approach we've been taking with Metal Gear Solid. We’ve been working on a fork of mgs_reversing (which is targeting 100% matching decompilation of MGS Integral) to bring the game natively to microcontrollers: https://github.com/davidmonterocrespo24/mgs_reversing

Instead of high-level emulation, the decompiled C source is compiled directly to Xtensa machine code for the ESP32-S3. We replaced the PlayStation SDK/GPU/GTE with custom software routines, running on a DIY handheld built around a Seeed XIAO ESP32-S3 Sense.

To speed up development without constantly flashing hardware, we run the compiled firmware image directly inside a browser-based hardware simulator CLI (velxio-cli) to verify serial outputs and execution in seconds.

Having 100% matching C code makes native ports to embedded platforms completely feasible without relying on heavy JIT/interpreter glue.

Hey guys,

If you've used Claude Tag, you know the potential of it for orchestration, a few months ago I built a version of it as a Claude Code plugin, that brings the concept as a local version of it, simply as a always-on task driven Claude Code agent. Our clis, our local memory, our filesystem, our tools, for you or your team.

It's how I manage and orchestrate several projects across different companies, and how I've been running always-on agents since. Set one up under 5m, it's just Claude Code so you can run with any subscription including 20$, it's fully customizable and it has got some magic focused on token efficiency using claude code native features:

1. Chat through Claude Code channels (Discord, Telegram, iMessage etc). Handle permission prompts in chat, recalls past conversations, keeps per-channel rules ("remember this for this channel"), has per-user allowlists for teams, and you manage the session from chat: !model, !effort, !clear, !compact, !stop, etc.

2. Routines that only wake Claude when needed. Each routine can run on its own model and effort, and a precheck script decides whether the model runs at all. Example: triage new GitHub issues hourly, with a gh CLI precheck that only wakes the model when there are new untriaged issues.

3. Heartbeat that only wakes Claude when there are pending stuff waiting, quiet ticks mean 0 tokens.

4. Spawn and orchestrate local Claude Code sessions with the model and effort you want and let it steer using cross-messaging. In chat each task has it's own thread and you can steer sessions per thread. You can also change !model and !effort on a thread session.

5. Take over the agent or any session on the CLI or the Claude app. (all of them start with remote-control)

6. A watchdog handles auto-restart, and context hygiene compacts long sessions and clears them when idle. All configurable.

Feel free to explore the repo for full list of features ;)

Contributions are welcome!

comment_text.value:
"Bad" is subjective, but as I stated, it's my opinion. It's not about work ethic at all; it's about your own values.

To simplify:

1. Reinforced behaviors become stronger, while others get weaker. Ultimately, I'm a behaviorist (ACT).

2. Work is a big part of your waking life.

3. If you spend that much of your life going through the motions, you're strengthening behaviors that may not be constructive.

4. When your situation changes, and you need those more constructive skills and behaviors, you may find them much more difficult to access.

That's a very functional lens. However, there's a deeper lens you can apply. I believe people feel most fulfilled when they're routinely acting in alignment with their core values (what they truly care about).

Phoning it in at work may actually be "workable" from an ACT standpoint if your personal life lights up all your values, and you are feeling completely fulfilled by friends, family, hobbies, etc.

However, I would venture that most people also want to feel that their work is giving them some feeling of intrinsic satisfaction, not just a paycheck. You can call it Purpose, Mission, Self-Efficacy, whatever you want. In my framing, people don't want to live in conflict with their values 8 hours/day.

But there's an even more basic argument that I would make: Life is incredibly short. You are hurtling toward death. If you're phoning it in, you're giving away your most precious resource for a small amount of financial security (and you still might get fired). You may find that when you hit 45 (or 65) you look back and weep for the decades you poured into something that you didn't care about, or even held in contempt.

You have to do what's right for you, but it's never too late. As someone who has admittedly phoned it in previously, I'm violently on the other side now. Regardless of how you feel about your job, I strongly recommend finding a way to give a shit, or getting out by any means necessary.

story_title.value: The Corporate Happiness Treadmill and the Case for Doing Less

This started when I spent twenty minutes trying to figure out whether Squeezits still exist (they don't - discontinued 2001). "Do they still make ..." turns out to be something everyone Googles, and the answers live in dead forum threads.

So I built a memorial: ~239 products so far, each with its lifespan, what killed it, and one verified odd fact (PB Max was reportedly killed despite ~$50M in sales because the owners disliked peanut butter). There's a "Gone or Still Here?" quiz - harder than it sounds, things keep resurrecting - and a random button.

Stack: Python static-site generator, JSON data, GitHub → Netlify. The content pipeline is the part I find interesting: AI-assisted research (Claude Code with a custom skill that mandates web fact-checking), but nothing publishes without passing a human review gate - early on the AI claimed a snack had been revived when it hadn't, which is exactly why the gate exists. In this niche, accuracy is the product: two weeks post-launch, Google is already routing question-clusters like "when were cheese nips discontinued" to the relevant page.

Happy to answer anything about the build or the model (boring long-game SEO + ads, in the spirit of odd single-purpose sites like IMCDB). And tell me what you miss - I'll research and add it.

story_title.value: Show HN: Dotheystillmake.com – a memorial archive of discontinued snacks
